library(ggplot2)
base_pth <- here::here("posts/2026-03-16-Lapras-Adventure")

> People have driven Lapras almost to the point of extinction. In the evenings, this Pokémon is said to sing plaintively as it seeks what few others of its kind still remain.
>
> -- Lapras entry in Pokemon Ruby and Sapphire

Ah, the rare and majestic Lapras. A pokemon so beloved by fans who were distraught at the news of its near extinction that later pokemon games have confirmed the conservation and repopulation of Lapras in the wild. My recent post-PhD adventures have involved quite a lot of free time that I didn't used to have, now that I'm out of academia and I have a job that respects my time and work contract. So I recently decided I wanted to play a new pokemon game, which is great because I loved [Emerald Seaglass](https://ko-fi.com/s/4a1535f351) and the final release of [Pokemon Lazarus](https://ko-fi.com/s/4baddcdbdc) by the same creator, Nemo622, was recently released to a nice amount of online hype. Something about the mildly not-quite-repetitive nature of filling out the PokeDex on my Pokemon Gym Challenge is very zen and relaxing for me, so I love playing ROM hacks and fan games with completable PokeDexes. (I don't have a Switch and I wasn't a big fan of Pokemon Sun, which was the last official title I played, so getting into fan games has been a great way to experience some awesome Pokemon content.)

My dex completion for Lazarus was coming along fine for quite a while. I tend to try to catch at least every wild pokemon and gift pokemon in an area before moving on (though I can't be bothered to grind out levels for a [Prof Oak Challenge](https://www.pokecommunity.com/threads/the-professor-oaks-challenge.501577/)). Then, I unlocked Surf and started trying to catch a Lapras. I know that Lapras is tradionally rare -- I started playing Pokemon in Gen 3, got the event Lapras in Leaf Green, and knew about the Sapphire pokedex entry. So I'm familiar with this rare and majestic sea beast. But then I kept searching and searching with no Lapras in sight. So I turned to the documentation to figure out the encounter rate and noted that it was 1%, the rarest encounter rate for a wild pokemon. I felt like I had done over 100 trials already, but I hadn't actually kept count, so I thought there was no way to know.

::: {#fig-pokes layout-ncol=2}
![Lapras](lapras.png){width=200}

![Shellder](shellder.png){width=200}

Lapras and Shellder, shown using their sprites from Pokemon Crystal.
:::

But I've been talking about proxy metrics at work a lot recently, and this was a big focus of my dissertation research. Anyone who knows about my professional career knows I'm very concerned with the way we take measurements. Anyways, I made another choice that happened to turn out very conveniently. I love Moxie [Honchkrow](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Honchkrow_(Pok%C3%A9mon)) and given the option I will almost always include one in my team in a Pokemon game -- this allows easy access to the move [Thief](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Thief_(move)) which can take the held items off of wild pokemon in battles. Since [Shellder](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Shellder_(Pok%C3%A9mon)) co-occurred in the same area where I was looking for Lapras and has a fairly high rate of dropping valuable items, I was using Thief to knock out every Shellder I came across. So after trying to find my Lapras for a while, I didn't know how many trials I had run (e.g. encounters generated in the same space), but I knew how many [Pearls](https://www.serebii.net/itemdex/pearl.shtml) and how many [Big Pearls](https://www.serebii.net/itemdex/bigpearl.shtml) were in my bag, and I knew I had zero before I started looking for Lapras in this zone. We also know the encounter rate for Lapras and Shellder, and the rate at which wild Shellder will hold Pearls and Big Pearls. Since the pokemon we encounter are disjoint, and the items Shellder can hold are disjoint, there's a fairly simple probability model here -- but instead of knowing how many trials we did and trying to estimate the rate at which something occurs, we know the rate at which everything occurs but not the number of trials we did.

So, given this framework, how do we estimate the number of trials?

## Estimating the number of trials

Alright, let's first describe a probability model for estimating the number of trials, in an abstract way. Once we've done that, we can fill in the parameters from the Pokemon Lazarus docs, write some R code, and get an estimate.

Let's consider the series of encounters
$$
\{X_T\} = \{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_t, \ldots, X_T\}.
$$

Here, $t = 1, \ldots, T; \quad T \in \mathbb{N}$ is a set of discrete time points and each $X_t$ is a pokemon encounter. At time $t$, we observe the variable $X_t$ whose sample space is

$$
\Omega_{X} = \{\text{all possible pokemon that can be found on the current tile}\}.
$$

For those who may not be familiar with how Pokemon works, the world is divided into a series of zones, and most zones have a few ways to encounter pokemon: each time you step into a grass tile, a cave (or other dangerous instance like a power plant) tile, or an ocean tile you have a random chance to encounter a wild pokemon. The wild pokemon you encounter is then randomly drawn from an encounter table that changes depending on the type of tile you're on, the zone you're in, and potentially other factors like the season or time of day in some games. (BTW if you aren't familiar with Pokemon, Lapras is pronounced like lap-ras not like la-prah.)

By structuring our random variable of interest as a discrete time series of encounters, we can ignore the random aspect of encounters -- the actual time between encounters doesn't matter to us, only the number of encounters. In this construction, the parameter $T$, the total number of encounters, is what is unknown to us.

Alright, now I'll dispense a bit with the formalism -- the proper notation for our sample space, domain of the random variable, etc. is not terribly important for what I want to talk about. All we really need to define to get this done is

$$
X_t = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if we encounter Lapras at encounter } t; \\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

We can then define $T = \min{t} \quad\text{s.t.}\quad X_t = 1$, i.e. we can stop generating new pokemon encounters once we find (and presumably catch, since I *am* a pokemon master, after all) a single Lapras. For now, we'll assume all of your encounters use the same encounter table, and thus that $p = \text{Pr}(X_t = 1) = 0.01 \quad\forall t$. This $0.01$ probability number is from the Pokemon Lazarus documentation.

In the absence of any other information, how do we estimate the number of trials? Well, let's do a little bit of variable manipulation so we can get this into a form with a known probability distribution. We can infer that the $X_t$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli with probability $p$, because there are only two options (success or failure), each event has exactly the same probability, and what happens at event $X_t$ gives us no new information about $X_s; \quad \forall t \neq s$ (i.e. the $X_t$ are all *mutually independent*.). This might make us want to define the sum of all $X_t$ as a binomial distribution --- which would be correct, except we already know that
$$\sum_{t=1}^T X_{t} = 1$$
because we know that trial $T$ is the first time we see an event occur! Now we can actually start with a binomial and get where I want to go, but worrying about derivations is not what I'm trying to do here, I don't have to mathematically prove anything to anyone in this blog post and I'm not turning it in for a grade.

So instead I can just say that **the distribution of the number of trials up to the first success** is the definition of a random variable that follows the [geometric distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_distribution). (Note the two parametrizations with different support in the first paragraph, I prefer the parametrization supported on $\mathbb{N}$.) So in this case, we can say that

$$T \sim \text{Geometric}(p).$$

That means we don't even really get to *estimate* $T$ here, we already know the full probability distribution of $T$ and we can directly compute the most probable values. Let's plot the distribution. Note that technically the support of $T$ is $\mathcal{S}_T = \mathbb{N}$, so technically $\text{Pr}(T = t) > 0 \quad \forall t in \mathbb{N}$, but for sufficiently large values of $t$, this probability is absurdly, monumentally small. A convenient cutoff for "real" probabilities is $\epsilon$, or "machine epsilon" -- the smallest difference between two numbers our computer can calculate. But that's a very small cutoff, so I'll just choose an arbitrary one of say $500$ encounters. Even without doing any math or looking at any plots, we can intuitively reason that if $p = 0.01$, or 1 in 100, $500$ would be a very unlikely number of encounters before seeing a single Lapras.

```{r}
p <- 0.01
t <- seq(1, 500, 1)
p_y <- dgeom(t, p)

ggplot(mapping = aes(x = t, y = p_y)) +
	geom_line() +
	labs(x = "t", y = "Pr(T = t)") +
	theme_minimal(base_size = 18)
```

Let's talk about this probability distribution a bit, because for me this is fairly unintuitive. We can see that the largest probability is at $t = 1$! But what does that mean?? In real life we would be shocked if we saw a $1\%$ Lapras as our first encounter in the zone! For me, this has to do with a mismatch between "the most likely single event" and "what we expect to happen if we repeat this process many times." The fact that $\text{Pr}(t = 1) = 0.01$ *can* be interpreted as "1 is the most probable value of $T$", which is true. But it also means something along the lines of "If we repeat the process of trying to catch a Lapras 100 times, we would expect to get Lapras in the first encounter only 1/100 times." Since there are infinitely many possibilities for how long it can take us to get Lapras (2, 3, 4, and so on), there is way more combined probability for larger numbers. We can think of the **mean** or **expected value** as the balance between these two facts. We can think of the expected value as the value we would get if we repeated our Lapras catching procedure infinitely many times (or, like, a million times or some other crazy big number) and took the average of all of the $T$ values. While it isn't *quite exactly* equivalent, this basically translates into "if we do a new run of our Lapras catching procedure and we have no other information, we should expect $T$ to be equal to its mean" --- hence why $E[T]$ or the mean is also called the expected value in statistics.

To calculate the mean of the probability distribution, we have a few options. First, you can just look at the formula on the wikipedia page, we've known what the mean of the geometric distribution is for at least a few hundred years. You can also derive it yourself if you know that

$$E[X] = \sum_{\mathcal{S}_X} x p(x)$$
